items.author: Zack Zwiezen

items.text:
A prominent PlayStation modder and hacker has had enough. He was working on a project to bring Linux to newer PS5 models running more recent firmware when he announced he was done with the entire PS5 hacking scene. The reason? A modder who uses AI tools admitted to sharing an important exploit with Sony after allegedly promising not to do so until the release of Grand Theft Auto 6. Now there’s a ton of drama in the community, and the future of the PS5 Linux mod, which turns the console into essentially a Steam Machine, is uncertain.

Earlier this year, longtime PlayStation hacker TheFlow shared a video of a modded PS5 running Linux and playing Grand Theft Auto 5. According to TheFlow, the Linux hack would only work on PS5 consoles running older firmware. But he eventually planned to get Linux to work on newer models, including the PS5 Pro, and make it compatible with the most recent firmware updates. A lot of people were excited about this possibility.

This Linux mod was possible thanks to an exploit TheFlow had discovered that involved the PS5’s hypervisor, a key piece of the console’s anti-piracy and anti-tampering security software. TheFlow didn’t want to share the updated Linux mod and this important exploit until after the release of GTA 6. That game’s digital-only release means that players will have to buy it using the PSN store, and to do that, you need to be on the most recent firmware from Sony. And once Sony learned about the exploit, TheFlow and others in the community knew it would be patched out via a new firmware update ASAP. So, to let people still buy and enjoy GTA 6 and also use the Linux PS5 hack, TheFlow was reportedly waiting and working on the mod, with a 2027 release likely planned.

However, on September 15, a different PS5 hacker named Jordy shared the same hypervisor exploit TheFlow was working on with Sony via HackerOne, a site that companies use to pay people who discover hacks and other exploits and share them privately with those companies. According to Jordy, who uses AI tools to help him mod and hack, TheFlow didn’t share the hypervisor exploit with him. Instead, Jordy claimed he had independently found it using his “trusty AI clanker machine,” and had been asked by TheFlow to not disclose it until after GTA 6‘s release.

When a third hacker also found the hypervisor exploit, Jordy reported it to Sony via HackerOne. He said he felt like it was only a matter of time before more people found it and tried to cash in on the bounty, which could pay out thousands of dollars if verified by PlayStation to be legitimate. Jordy’s mother is reportedly suffering from a terminal illness, and many in the community believe he could really use the money.

TheFlow is done with PS5 hacking

But now others are frustrated that the hypervisor exploit will likely be patched out in the near future. As a result of Jordy reporting the exploit to HackerOne, TheFlow posted that he’s walking away from the PS5 hacking and modding scene entirely.

“I am stepping away from the PS5 scene and stopping all my work on PS5 Linux,” posted TheFlow. “After pouring my heart and months of my life into it, including plans to finish PS5 Pro support and release in 2027, it’s all down the sink. The scene used to be a group of highly talented researchers, but now it is just a bunch of noobs using LLMs and writing hacks they don’t even understand. Slop kiddies found the only hypervisor bug left, which I had also found a while ago, and decided to report to Sony.”

In his tweets, TheFlow doesn’t specify who he is talking about, but many in the community believe it to be Jordy, who had already posted previously about talking to TheFlow and being asked to not report the exploit. TheFlow also claims that the person he’s referring to had agreed to wait, but then a day later went back on this promise. Jordy himself has confirmed he was asked by TheFlow to not report the exploit, but after someone else found it, he reported it.

“Wow, woke up to some drama tldr the [hypervisor] bug I reported to [HackerOne] is TheFlow’s,” posted Jordy on Tuesday on Twitter. “He asked me to not report it, and I said I wouldn’t, and then someone found the bug with AI a few hours later, so I reported it.” Jordy also shared a screenshot allegedly showing someone in the community sending him a nasty message about his mother dying.

The whole situation has led to a lot of online debating between PS5 jailbreak community members and hackers, with some people picking Team Jordy or Team TheFlow.

As some see it, Jordy has handed Sony a valuable exploit that would have let many people turn their PS5s into open-source Linux computers while still being able to play GTA 6. Others feel Jordy didn’t do anything wrong because he discovered the hypervisor exploit himself and reported it to get money he desperately needs. And others still have pointed out that some in the community will likely keep working on the Linux PS5 project to get it running on more models; it just might take a lot longer now. Some wished Jordy (or TheFlow) had taken a community-funded $37,000+ bounty for a hypervisor exploit that would have kept the info away from Sony, though this likely would have caused issues for either hacker with continuing to claim PlayStation bounties on HackerOne.

One popular post on the PS5 Jailbreak subreddit simply shows the meme image of a young girl looking at a house on fire. She’s labeled as Sony, and the house is the PS5 hacking scene. The top reply to that comment is “I guess doing nothing paid off on Sony’s part and let the scene devour itself.” On Wednesday, Sony pushed out a new PS5 firmware update. Many in the community, including Jordy, warned players who want to continue jailbreaking and hacking their consoles to not update.

Published Sep 17, 2026, 6:05 AM EDT

Ewan is Deputy Editor for ScreenRant's gaming section. He still quite hasn’t gotten out of his mid 00’s emo phase, and knows more about The Legend of Zelda and Doctor Who than is probably healthy.
Ewan oversees the content operation of ScreenRant's gaming output, working with a talented team of writers and editors to cover everything from the latest GTA 6 news to the indie games you need on your radar.
Former Editor of GAMINGbible, Ewan also has words at Kotaku, Den of Geek, NME, and UNILAD. He's appeared on various podcasts, including VGC's and BBC's Let's Talk About Tech.

These days, gamers like to complain that video games are frequently released in a buggy or unfinished state. They're not entirely wrong. We know that developers can simply patch out any issues with regular updates — just look at Cyberpunk 2077 or No Man's Sky now compared to launch. But what I think a lot of younger gamers don't realize is that back in the 80s, 90s, and early 00s, games were still being released that were clearly unfinished. The only difference was they had to stay that way forever.

Over the years, we've seen some genuine clunkers put out there that were barely playable when they released, and haven't exactly gotten any better with age. Take a walk with me, as we look at some of the most unplayable video games to have ever seen the light of day.

A game so bad it nearly sent the entire video game industry down the toilet before it ever had a chance to get going. Released for the Atari 2600 in 1982, it was a confusing mess of a game that made a trip to the dentist seem like a day at Disneyland by comparison. Sales were so poor that millions of unsold cartridges were dumped in a landfill in the desert.

If you've ever wondered why video games based on movies are usually awful, my theory is because this one somehow put a curse on its descendants.

9
Custer's Revenge (1982)

There aren't many video games that are genuinely evil, but Custer's Revenge is definitely one of them. An unlicensed Atari 2600 game, it's based (very loosely) on 19th century American General George Armstrong Custer and the Battle of the Little Bighorn. The fact that the game is awful to play isn't even the worst thing about it: it's simply horrific and cruel on pretty much every level, with its greatest sin being that the entire premise of the game centers around the player character moving from one side of the screen to the other to sexually assault a Native American woman. Yes, it's just a crude mess of pixels, but the intent of the game is still clear, which is why we can't even show you a screenshot. Even if you could play this in 2026, you shouldn't.

8
Dr. Jekyll And Mr Hyde (1988)

A game based on the classic Robert Luos Stevenson novel The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde sounds like a pretty cool concept. It was released for the Nintendo Entertainment System, and even looked a bit like the gothic platformer Castlevania on the surface, which is a solid place for a Jekyll and Hyde game to draw inspiration from. Alas, it is nothing like as good as Castlevania. Then again, it's also nothing like as good as dipping your face in a bucket of acid, so the bar is very much on the floor.

Multiple reviewers over the years have referred to this game as unplayable, thanks to its confusing levels and frustrating design choices that make it a needlessly difficult experience. Throw in some horrendous controls and you have a winner. By which I mean you have a loser.

7
Shaq Fu (1994)

A fighting game starring American basketball legend Shaquille O'Neal isn't an instant no from me. And, to be fair, the game received mixed reviews at launch rather than outright vitriol. However, over time, this Super Nintendo and SEGA Genesis game has come to be regarded as a cynical and shallow cash-grab best left forgotten. There's even a website dedicated to destroying every single copy of Shaq Fu, which seems like a bit of an overreaction.

But is it unplayable? After over four decades of fighting games, it kind of is, yeah. We've been spoiled over the years with luxuries like responsive controls, compelling rosters of fighters, and engaging gameplay. Shaq Fu offers none of this, and less. Shaq Fu: A Legend Reborn was released in 2018, but the remaster got dunked on even harder than the original.

6
Zelda's Adventure (1996)

Nintendo really doesn't want you to remember this, but there were actually three Zelda games released back in the 90's for a doomed multimedia console called the Philips CD-i. All three of them are truly dreadful, but the worst of the bunch is Zelda's Adventure. On paper, a top-down Zelda game where you actually get to play as the Princess sounds great! The recent Echoes of Wisdom certainly proved it can work.

Ewan is Deputy Editor for ScreenRant's gaming section. He still quite hasn’t gotten out of his mid 00’s emo phase, and knows more about The Legend of Zelda and Doctor Who than is probably healthy.
Ewan oversees the content operation of ScreenRant's gaming output, working with a talented team of writers and editors to cover everything from the latest GTA 6 news to the indie games you need on your radar.
Former Editor of GAMINGbible, Ewan also has words at Kotaku, Den of Geek, NME, and UNILAD. He's appeared on various podcasts, including VGC's and BBC's Let's Talk About Tech.

Between PlayStation confirming that it's moving towards an all-digital future, and Rockstar Games admitting GTA 6 will never be released on disc, it's a pretty concerning time to be a gamer. I probably don't need to remind you, but just in case: we technically don't own digital games. What you purchase when you buy a digital game is a license to access the software, and that access can be revoked.

So, since we live in an age where some games can apparently just vanish off the face of the Earth one day, I thought now would be as good a time as any to look at five Square Enix games that are impossible (or near-enough impossible) to access and play in 2026. Because if this can happen with a company like Square Enix, it can happen with any publisher.

Babylon's Fall (2022)

An action-RPG from Square Enix and developed by PlatinumGames should have been a big hit on paper. Unfortunately, for whatever reason, Babylon's Fall failed to capture the attention of players. Maybe the reason is that Square Enix attempted to sell us what was effectively a live-service game for the price of a AAA single-player RPG. We'll never know for sure.

To say the launch was a disaster would be an understatement. Square Enix pulled Babylon's Fall from sale in 2022, and then wiped server access and gameplay data in February 2023. Yikes. It is now fully inaccessible, though I'm not sure the world weeps for this one.

NieR Re[in]carnation (2021)

While NieR Reincarnation isn't really a patch on the main games in the series, this free-to-play mobile RPG still had the legendary Yoko Taro at the helm, and offered a rich world to explore and plenty of deep lore to uncover. Unfortunately, as is so often the way with live-service gacha games, it stopped making enough money to justify the cost of running servers or continuing development. The game was terminated in 2024, and there's no offline version available. At least, there's no official offline version, but you didn't hear that from us.

Marvel's Avengers (2020)

Marvel's Avengers wanted to be the kind of game you could play for years, and as such, a promising single-player action game was stretched into an ugly and repetitive series of missions. New stories featuring the likes of Black Panther and Spider-Man ultimately couldn't save this game, and it quickly became clear it could not, to borrow a phrase from Captain America, do this all day.

Servers were shut down on September 30, 2023, and the game was delisted from digital storefronts. You can still track down physical copies, however, and play through the game's single-player campaign. Honestly, it's worth picking up just for this.

Final Fantasy VII: Ever Crisis (2023)

Okay, so support for this ends on October 6, 2026, so it's technically still playable at the moment. But once it's gone later this year, that's your lot... consider this one a warning. Final Fantasy VII: Ever Crisis is basically a retelling of the entire Final Fantasy VII saga for mobile devices.

Over the course of multiple updates over the years, it's gone over the events of the original Final Fantasy VII, multiple spinoff games, and movies. If this game proves anything, it's that maybe there's such a thing as too much Final Fantasy VII. As for why it's shutting down? Same as any of the others: it stopped making enough money.

Final Fantasy: All the Bravest (2013)

Of all the games listed here, this one had the best run by far. Final Fantasy: All The Bravest was released in 2013, and finally shut down on iOS in July 2023 and Android in November 2022. If you've never heard of it, All The Bravest was a touch-screen action-RPG for mobile devices with a pixel art-style and characters from across Final Fantasy history. It is, I am afraid, largely considered to be a stinker of a game due to fact it was incredibly boring to play. That it struggled on for as long as it did is kind of amazing, but it was ultimately taken offline due to intense backlash to the game's monetization features and dwindling player numbers.

items.text:
I had an extremely good time with the Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter last year. As a big fan of the Trails of Cold Steel PC ports, finally getting the opportunity to try the first installment in the beloved JRPG series, with all the modern accoutrements of a full 3D remake, was truly a pleasure.

Falcom really didn't skimp when it came to upgrading the experience to the standard of its newer Trails games. There's only one problem: I wanted more.

Despite 1st Chapter being a pretty well-rounded story—clocking in at a perfectly reasonable 40 hours for me—it ends on a criminal cliffhanger. It's easy to see why so many say that 2nd Chapter is really just the second part of the first game, something I probably should've clocked considering the naming convention.

But having played Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter Remake this last week or so, I can say it feels more like a victory lap, building on the setting, characters, and quests you completed in the first. It's very much what you'd expect from the middle child of a JRPG trilogy—the cogs are turning, the characters moving, we're going somewhere.

2nd Chapter's Bracer requests feel a bit trickierFalcomWith save import, many characters from the first game will remember youFalcomThe banter is also extremely goodFalcomLots of great character momentsFalcomOlivier and Estelle's relationship continues to be my favFalcomWhile I won't spoil too much, 2nd Chapter feels like a bit more of a coming of age story for Estelle, as she finds herself adrift as a newly-made Senior Bracer. With the help of familiar faces, you'll travel around Liberl investigating the activities of Ouroborous, the secret society who reared their head in the previous game.

So yes, it's the classic Trails recipe: cosy and comfy odd-jobbing as you help the citizens of Liberl, but with a dash of uncovering and foiling grand nefarious schemes. I'm about 30 hours into 2nd Chapter, but it feels very much like your typical Trails game in that sense—good news if that's what you like. I know I do.

There are a few improvements that jumped out at me, though, having played the 1st Chapter Remake so recently:

The Bracer requests and puzzles are a lot better. I had one where I had to fix a lighthouse by reading a manual, another where I undertook a criminal investigation, and another where I literally had to beat a guy at poker, all which I could've failed.

The new combat and craft animations look really good, both in terms of characters and bosses, who now have S-breaks.

The party rostering is much improved. Though I love characters popping up and then disappearing JRPG-style, 2nd Chapter does a much better job of giving you a consistent roster and more character choice. Early in the game you'll even get to choose between two semi-permanent party members.

You may often be revisiting the same locations, but it's nice that the quests you completed also carry over from your 1st Chapter save data. There are so many NPCs you'll bump into who'll be like "Oh, I remember you helping my gran find her hearing aid." But the situation in each region will also feel different, like the story of Liberl has moved forward.

FalcomFalcomAnd, of course, you've got the same excellent character banter. Estelle is on top form, but I genuinely found myself getting engrossed in her emotional turmoil, yet drive to fight for the truth and closure. Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter isn't as revolutionary as 1st Chapter was, but it's a strong sequel that certainly builds on what made the first remake so good.

If you want to play it yourself, it's out on September 17, or you can try the Steam demo first. You can also play the demo for the 1st Chapter, which is currently 50% off—I assume to coincide with 2nd Chapter's release.

There are a few improvements that jumped out at me, though, having played the 1st Chapter Remake so recently:

The Bracer requests and puzzles are a lot better. I had one where I had to fix a lighthouse by reading a manual, another where I undertook a criminal investigation, and another where I literally had to beat a guy at poker, all which I could've failed.
The new combat and craft animations look really good, both in terms of characters and bosses, who now have S-breaks.

The party rostering is much improved. Though I love characters popping up and then disappearing JRPG-style, 2nd Chapter does a much better job of giving you a consistent roster and more character choice. Early in the game you'll even get to choose between two semi-permanent party members.

You may often be revisiting the same locations, but it's nice that the quests you completed also carry over from your 1st Chapter save data. There are so many NPCs you'll bump into who'll be like "Oh, I remember you helping my gran find her hearing aid." But the situation in each region will also feel different, like the story of Liberl has moved forward.

FalcomFalcomAnd, of course, you've got the same excellent character banter. Estelle is on top form, but I genuinely found myself getting engrossed in her emotional turmoil, yet drive to fight for the truth and closure. Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter isn't as revolutionary as 1st Chapter was, but it's a strong sequel that certainly builds on what made the first remake so good.

If you want to play it yourself, it's out on September 17, or you can try the Steam demo first. You can also play the demo for the 1st Chapter, which is currently 50% off—I assume to coincide with 2nd Chapter's release.

items.title: Tim Willits doesn't think Rideshare's generative AI is damaging Saber's reputation
items.author: Julian Benson
items.summary: A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z,
items.text:
A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z, the company was dealing with the shitstorm that ensued from their announcement of Rideshare Stimulator.

The game's basically an Uber simulator, with you driving a car around town picking up fares, but Saber drew all kinds of bad attention when a former writer on the game revealed the game featured generative AI (something left undisclosed on the game's Steam page until recently) and CEO Matt Karch responded by attacking the writer in statements to the press. Something he has since apologised for.

So, naturally, we talked about generative AI and the reputational damage – or lack of – when getting caught out using it.

Watch on YouTube

Rideshare will have a main narrative, similar to other simulator games, in which you start your business in a city and grow it up as you complete jobs. Similar to something you would play through in Snowrunner. "All that is written by humans, all the missions are written by humans," Willits tells me. Where the generative AI appears is in Rideshare's Free Ride mode.

In Free Ride, when you pick up a fare, their dialogue will be generated using an LLM. "What we want to do is feed current events, like maybe there's some soccer game, and some ride will get in and talk about it," Willits explains. He says Saber are "using it here in a small part of a small game to test the waters." and that the company are "interested in how AI can help in games."

Willits says Rideshare is the only game in which Saber are using generative AI – "We don't have AI in Space Marine. We don't have AI in Hellraiser. We don't have AI in Jurassic Park, but we want to figure it out and we want to try something."

When I spoke with Willits, the thing I most wanted to know was why there was no AI disclosure on the Rideshare's Steam page when it was first revealed. Valve have a clear policy on disclosing the use of generative AI both in the production of a game and if any feature of the game makes ongoing calls to LLMs.

The reason, Willits says, is they "had an announce plan, but that got a little sideways". There was going to be a sneak peak, then there would have been reveals of the game's features in the future, and as part of that the generative technology would have been revealed. To indicate how early in the game's reveal rollout they are, Willits points out Rideshare's "not here" at Gamescom. "Unfortunately, we had some people talk about the game when they weren't supposed to be talking about the game and that just kind of escalated."

Though, I bring it back to Valve's AI disclosure policy because it doesn't make a distinction between whether a feature has been announced or not, only whether the technology is used in a game. Shouldn't the disclosure still have been there when the game was announced? "Okay, sure," Willits says.

The point I'm building to with Willits is that by not initially disclosing the use of AI, it seeds doubt about generative AI's use in Saber's other games. The tool may have been used but the company is not yet ready to announce or reveal it. I point to another of Saber's games, Road Kings, a new American trucking simulator which I really enjoyed at a preview event in April. While on the road, other drivers or job brokers may message you to ask for help, spurring an emergent quest. Certainly, there's no suggestion that these quests are generated by AI, but to a player the two systems could appear similar and they may now question 'Is this generative AI Saber's not copped to yet?'. "You may be overthinking it a little bit," Willits says. "I wouldn't worry about that. Again, the wishlists are up, interest is up, preorders across our games are up."

I didn't want to move on immediately, as Road Kings captures the issue well. I saw the game back in April but its embargo for the preview only came up after the Rideshare story had broken. I played and enjoyed that game and its mix of American Truck Simulator-style hauling blended with scenes you might see in a disaster move like Twister. But the comments on the preview were largely about the Rideshare news and Saber's use of AI. Willits, again, disagrees this is an issue. "I wouldn't really worry about that," he says. "The games will speak for themselves. You enjoyed Road Kings. The people that play it, they will enjoy it. I've been in the industry for 30 whatever years, you will always get crazy comments."

Willits points back to when he was working at id and they announced Quake 3 would need a video card to play. "We were roasted," he says. "The internet hate was crazy. 'You're ruining the industry. How can you make me pay $100 for a video card?' – imagine a $100 video card! – But the game came out and people liked it."

Willits also points to the launch of Steam, which, while a well-regarded platform now, was not universally loved at launch. In part because its servers struggled and its online functionality demanded more from peoples' internet than a lot of dial up and early broadband connections could provide. "I think we're in a period now of technology change that people are really unsure about," Willits says. "We, as game developers, don't really know what we're doing with it yet. Players don't really know what's going on with it. But I do think that there will be a game from somebody that will be so awesome that everyone will be like 'That's it. Now I get it.' I think the games will speak for themselves and when people play or they read your stories, and they watch the videos and they see the content, they will make their own determination."

As I've said in the past to other developers, I can believe there are ways these new AI technologies could benefit my work. For instance, the first transcription pass of most my interviews is done automatically because I use Google's Recorder app. But I also know the worst thing I could do with [insert AI tool of your choice] would be to generate an article for RPS. No one comes to this site to see something cobbled together by an LLM, they want something lovingly stitched together by these dyslexic typo-spewing hands. So I ask Willits what he thinks the benefit for Saber will be.

"As a game developer, if you're going to try something with brand new generative AI, it's much better to try it with something small [rather] than your biggest title," Willits says. "For us, part of our strategy at Saber is to make our mega hits – Space Marine 3, Jurassic Park, Turok – but we have to have smaller games that are consistent when it comes to how long it takes to make, how much money they make, [that's where] we experiment with things. Look at Spintires. That was an experiment that turned into a mega franchise. Rideshare fits into that category. It is a Rideshare simulator, where you drive around and you pick people up. There's really not much more you can really do there. And so for us, we wanted to be like 'Well, let's try this. Let's try it here because if it doesn't work out, it's on that game. It's not on our mega hits.'"

In the case of Rideshare's Free Ride mode, Willits says "This is a gameplay feature that is not possible without this technology. It would be logistically too hard, it'd be so expensive. We'd have to have an army." And, as he's described it, a mode where passenger dialogue is generated in response to current events fed into the game, I agree. Either you would have a madlibs style system of words being swapped in and out of repeating schemas, or a human writer adding additional lines in response to real world news events.

I do want to see if Saber are able to produce anything better than the other games that have stuck LLMs inside the throats of their characters. In Where Winds Meet, players quickly convinced one of the NPCs that they were pregnant, and another to provide cooking advice for potatoes and ketchup. That implementation and others were panned by developers Samuel Horti spoke to back in December.

My experience of generative AI dialogue has largely been formulaic and predictable. Which, could make for incredibly dreary car journeys. Ironically, the last taxi ride I was in I told the driver he was taking us to an engagement meal and he told me how AI was going to destroy the world by 2030.

Travel and accommodation to Gamescom was provided by the conference organisers.

items.title: "We track every server you enter": the Wardogs devs are "coming down hard" on XP farms and cash exploits, even as they encourage people to grind
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: The creators of military shooter Wardogs have announced that they will crack down heavily on players who use exploits and bugs to speedily farm in-game
items.text:
The creators of military shooter Wardogs have announced that they will crack down heavily on players who use exploits and bugs to speedily farm in-game currency and XP, or who spend “more than a few minutes” in servers created for this purpose.

Given that Wardogs advertises itself as a shooter about getting rich – a game in which "cash is king", with individualised payouts for a bunch of different in-game actions - I do feel like Bulkhead are sending mixed messages, even by the standards of incoherent wargames. Trying to define 'fairly earned' in a game that encourages you to be a frenzied, gun-toting plutomaniac is surely plunging headfirst into farce. Mind you, I respect the desire to Maintain The Fun for players who aren't quite as dollar-driven, and avoid having a community browser slammed with servers called "[EU/DOGF$RM]" or similar.

Wardogs launched in early access last week, reaching an audience of over 400,000 simultaneous Steam players by Sunday. James spent some time in it last week, and returned with many thrilling gigwork anecdotes. The devs have now rolled out a patch aimed at improving the game's server browser, with a new dedicated feed for community servers.

"Community Servers are the lifeblood of FPS games like ours," they write on Steam. "We want to make sure we actively create technology in and out of the game that supports the growth and fostering of communities. We have failed to do that by rushing our Community Server strategy. As we've always said, when we're wrong, we'll hold our hands up. We got this bit wrong." In addition to the update, the devs are giving players in community servers an additional 5% End of Match cash bonus by way of apology. "So if you're looking to grind, we suggest jumping in a community server."

These heartwarming sentiments about server grinding go hand in hand with a blood-chilling threat against those who create or join servers purely in order to crank out XP by mindlessly repeating actions. "The economy of WARDOGS interlinks all players together into one shared universe and experience, even more so when we bring the meta into the game," the devs write. "As an early access game, we're not perfect, and we never will be. But if you do find something and take advantage of it, we have decided to come down hard."

Players who "abuse cash exploits and bugs" will have their cash and XP reset to zero. You'll also get a timed ban, depending on previous infractions. People who make "content that tutorialises how to abuse systems, with no regard for reporting the issue" will be treated "as advertising cheats", and will receive a permanent ban. The wording here is a bit muddy, but it sounds like they're telling us not to share details about cash/XP exploits, unless we're genuinely trying to report an issue to the devs. "We are not saying do not post on social media or Discord," the devs write. "We are saying there is a difference between promoting and alerting."

And people who launch or make use of XP server farms? For you Bulkhead have unlocked the very lowest echelons of Banhammer Hell. "We track every server you enter, and we are also very aware of which servers are XP farming servers," they write. "If your account is tracked as joining one of these servers for more than a few minutes, we will ban your account permanently."

Bulkhead promise that even if you're currently getting away with abusing a system, they'll catch up to you eventually. "Effectively, if you find something and you then keep doing it, over and over again, that is abuse of an exploit," they conclude. "If you figure something out and test it once or twice, no biggy, thanks for helping us QA."

Bulkhead are hardly unique in wanting people to obsess over an in-game earning loop, but not to the extent that they take the logical next step, game the system, and mess up the experience for other players. The creators of Destiny have had this discussion a billion times over. It just amuses me a bit more in a game that has all this edgelord materialism up front. It's a dog-eat-dog world out there but stop that! Bad dog! You must play by the agreed rules. Anyway: have you spent any time in Wardogs? I don't know if James plans to keep up his combat taxi-driving career.

Published Sep 17, 2026, 5:40 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

Released back in 2023 as the sequel to Breath of the Wild, The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom was as much of a success as its predecessor. Known by fans as the 'Wilds' saga, both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom put a brand-new spin on the Zelda franchise, offering fans a sprawling open-world and a painterly art style to boot.

Whilst some fans prefer the more cel-shaded visuals of classic Zelda entries, there is no denying that the Nintendo Switch series has been a hit, with the sequel hitting a massive 10 million copies sold within three days.

Here at Screen Rant, we also praised The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, awarding it a 10/10 in our review. As such, our very own Cody Gravelle had the following to say:

While most complaints about Tears of the Kingdom will largely be seen as small ones, that's just the bar the game sets for itself. It may not be perfect, but it's every bit as absorbing as its predecessor, with a world that feels even more dizzying in its grandeur.

Now that Nintendo is moving on from the Wilds duology in order to work on the November release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, it seems as though there is one last ditch attempt to bring people back to Tears of the Kingdom over three years on from its initial launch.

Launching today, 17 September, Zelda fans can get their hands on a brand-new Amiibo dedicated to The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. The Mineru's Construct Amiibo retails at $34.99 and, as with any Amiibo, it will come alongside a code which, when scanned, will add some downloadable content to your game.

"She is King Rauru's elder sister and helped her brother fight the Demon King in her role as the Sage of Spirit long ago. She now helps Link in the present day through this Zonai construct," the official item description reads.

"This figure has articulated arms that you can move around and pose how you like. It also lets you receive random items in the Hyrule Warriors: Age of Imprisonment, The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild, and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom games. You may even receive a special fabric for Link's paraglider in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom."

As you can see, there are plenty of in-game rewards to get your hands on upon purchasing the brand-new Amiibo. Simply purchase it and scan the accompanying code to the NFC touchpoint in order to join all of the brand-new DLC.

It remains to be seen why Nintendo has released DLC for The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom so long after its launch, but hey, if you have been debating another playthrough, or have yet to get started, this may just be the incentive you need.

items.text:
Need to know

What is it? Rule-breaking sci-fantasy 4X
Release date: September 17, 2026 (1.0 version)
Expect to pay: $50/£45
Developer: Amplitude Studios
Publisher: Hooded Horse
Reviewed on: Radeon RX 6800 XT, Ryzen 9 5900, 32GB RAM
Steam Deck: Verified
Link: Official site

There has been no drought of good 4X games over the past decade. Part of that has been the steady work of Amplitude, whose Endless series has become a stalwart part of the strategy scene. Endless Legend 2 further cements Amplitude's legacy as a great 4X developer, delivering the studio's trademark creativity and standout visual design in a modernized package.

The original Endless Legend was a shot in the arm for a 4X genre that had gotten pretty stale. If you'd asked me in the years afterward if I wanted more Endless Legend, I'd have said yes. In the years since, many of its innovations—and those from sibling series Endless Space—have become standards in the genre. You might expect that to have dulled some of the charm. 12 years later, though, I still want more Endless Legend.

Sciences fantastical

I wanted more Endless Legend because there's never enough good science fantasy. Not the Star Wars kind, though that's fun too, but the kind where it's sword and sorcery with a technological flavor. Where it's mostly monsters and wizards. Bows, not blasters.

So I'm glad that we're back to Endless Legend's worlds of crashed starship survivors building robotic golems and battling with titanium swords and wielding magic that might just be nanotechnology. The setting and its weird people are just as good as the first time, though a bit more scientific-feeling. No dragons, for example, or elf stand-ins—instead we've got evolved desert lizards, coral robots, and sand spirit genies. It's another rich world that lets its developers break the rules of the genre in interesting and creative ways.

(Image credit: Amplitude Studioss)The shoreline recedes, unveiling sunken landscapes and ancient technologies that are now ripe for your faction to colonize and exploit.

The new world of Saiadha is familiar in one important way: Like Auriga of Endless Legend, Saiadha is dying. This time though it's because the Endless, an ancient race, sealed something away beneath Saiadha when they terraformed it from a planet of desert dunes into one of storm-wracked seas and isolated islands. Now that something is coming back, which means the oceans are draining away into the planet's core.

Every few dozen turns a monsoon comes, shrouding the world in storms, and at the end of that monsoon season comes Tidefall: The shoreline recedes, unveiling sunken landscapes and ancient technologies that are now ripe for your faction to colonize and exploit—a perfect setup for a genre about expanding and building.

Aesthetics fantastical

Endless Legend 2 continues the tradition of the first game in another way with one of the most pleasing, coherent aesthetics in the entire strategy game space. The painterly color choices across terrain and units, both matte and gloss, make different areas of the world and the new biomes that emerge from the ocean very distinct.

Endless Legend 2 also makes very good use of texture on terrain to convey types of earth, sand, grass, stone, or even a field of vast living circuitry. My major critique is that the lighting is quite flat—it really only changes during monsoons—and something more dynamic or directional might have helped highlight the models and environments. Better to have simple lighting than effects that muddy the visual environment, though.

(Image credit: Amplitude Studioss)While it's still a best-in-genre user interface, interacting with Endless Legend 2 doesn't feel as aesthetically pleasing and crisp as the first game. The redesigned resource displays, menus bar, and action wheels are good, but the use of symbols on the map for cities and armies rather than clear, obvious text labels conveys less information while making the player do more work to understand what they're looking at. I had issues distinguishing the symbols for cities, armies, and resource locations until I learned where each was located. A temporary annoyance, but bad friction nonetheless.

The highlight for many will be yet another standout soundtrack from Arnaud Roy. Ethereal at times—subdued and ambient—it makes extensive use of a crystal organ. What most impressed me was how it changes as you go, avoiding repetitive loops and adapting dynamically to the screen you're on or what's happening in a battle round. Opening a diplomacy screen, for example, seems to dull out or soften the bass parts so you can hear the faction leader characters speak clearly.

Play fantastical

What may disappoint some about Endless Legend 2 is that many of the first game's signature innovations have become routine. Ideas like changing or terraforming the map, or your cities expanding over large regions, have been adopted by many others in the genre. The signature Amplitude resource system is present in full and simple to understand: Incomes for cities—FIDSI for Food, Industry, Dust, Science, and Influence—with tradeable luxury resource stockpiles for upgrades and everything else. Some might be bored of it, but it works really well, and I don't think you should mess with a good system.

What is still superb is how Amplitude wants every faction to break the rules in some way, repeating only a few tricks from Endless Legend or Endless Space. Particularly fresh is how Saiadha's receding oceans play into the genre tropes of a 4X.

(Image credit: Amplitude Studioss)It throws you back into the most exciting and interesting parts of the 4X genre multiple times throughout a typical length game.

The genre is at its best during two phases—the initial exploration and expansion, and the secondary squabble and race over who will control resources and which factions will actually fight with each other for them. Endless Legend's system of neutral territories is perfect for this, as you can stake claims by building camps, but must be wary of attack from enemies or marauding minor factions who can burn those down without declaring an official war.

The worst part of most 4X is when the map stagnates, empires get huge, and you engage in a grind toward whatever finish line you're aiming for. In Endless Legend 2, every time the seas recede and new land appears, the shorelines change—previously isolated territories may connect to each other, precious deposits or strategic resources may appear, and new dungeons for your heroes to delve or undiscovered minor factions may show up. Tidefall means your previously safe border may become vulnerable, or that your worst city is now part of a rich new frontier. In short, it throws you back into the most exciting and interesting parts of the 4X genre multiple times throughout a typical length game.

Tactics fantastical

The changing map also means your armies are in constant motion. You always want them moving from place to place, scouting out new territory, gathering curiosities, and either fighting or doing quests for neutral minor factions. At the same time you need them to guard your borders against potential aggressors, or against the terrible Doomwraiths that come each monsoon season, and you want them in position for the next tidefall. Where your military units and scouts are just map decoration in some 4X games, in Endless Legend 2 they're hooked into every part of the game loop in a way that feels like part of the exploration and wonder of a good fantasy story.

(Image credit: Amplitude Studioss)4X games are rarely well-tuned, but I found that the settings in Endless Legend 2 actually worked very well on their defaults.

For all that, the tactical combat is perhaps less rich than I'd like it to be. The positioning elements of the turn-based fights are as good as ever, especially because of how it happens across the natural game map. You carefully position your armies to attack enemies from favorable terrain. As a faction like the Tahuks, who rely on ranged combat and want to exploit chokepoints, or the Sandshapers, who want to fight on desert terrain whenever possible, controlling space by positioning is still very good.

What leads to it feeling less rich is that it's very tightly wound—damage numbers are such that fights are nearly equal exchanges unless you outnumber the enemy 2:1, and scraping out an advantage often feels like exploiting the system by stacking buffs or abusing the terrain.

That said, 4X games are rarely well-tuned, but I found that the difficulty settings in Endless Legend 2 actually worked very well on their defaults. Higher settings actually delivered greater difficulty in consistent, measured steps, and the highest difficulties were so rough that you could end up in wholly unwinnable starts at times, which paradoxically I'd count as a real success.

That success, however, is still achieved by inflating the AI factions' abilities with bonus resources rather than making them better at playing the game. So sometimes the only way to win those tight tactical combats against a stream of armies you could never out-produce was by abusing the heck out of a system.

Weirdos fantastical

The factions are the highlight of this game, as with any Endless game, because of how asymmetrical they are. Each of them breaks or ignores some fundamental game mechanic.

Whether it's the Children of Sheredyn who'd rather build a fortress than a public plaza, or the Sandshapers, living mineral constructs who can't farm and must scrape together rare resources and terraform the world back into desert in order to gather the minerals they need to produce new population. There are even two "rogue" variants of factions that invert their primary playstyle—the defensive Sheredyn become an aggressive expansionist legion, the devouring Necrophage become an enslaving swarm of cyborgs.

(Image credit: Amplitude Studioss)There's less extremity than in Endless Legend in places—no faction can move its cities, for example—but there's still wild stuff in here that would be seen as unacceptable in other games. The friendly Aspects, a symbiosis of living corals and robotics, can spend their copious influence to force treaties like peace or trade on other factions. The Necrophage can only have one city, their hive, and are always justified in declaring war on others. (They're hungry, OK?)

There's just not another 4X where you can play as religious fanatic lizards who use a solar mirror laser to turn the world to glass. I appreciate that.

items.author: clivingston@pcgamer.com (Christopher Livingston)

items.text:
Zach Cregger's Resident Evil movie comes out this week on September 18, and the early reviews have just dropped. It's good news for games and horror fans: it sounds like just about everyone likes it, with more than one reviewer calling it the best videogame adaptation ever made.

(That's a pretty low bar, but still.)

Granted, early reviewers are hand-picked by studios, so it pays to take these first batch of glowing reviews with a grain of salt—and speaking of salty, PC Gamer (despite asking nicely a number of times!) wasn't granted a press screening, so we can't offer our own take. I know, boo hoo, poor us. In the meantime, until we get a chance to see it ourselves, you can get hyped by what a bunch of other outlets have said about the latest Resident Evil flick:

GamesRadar+ (4/5): "Turns out eighth time's a charm, as despite much pre-release griping over the absence of iconic game characters like Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, director Zach Cregger's Resident Evil isn't just the best Resi movie by a distance; it's the best video game movie full stop," says Jordan Farley.

Polygon (91/100): "Cregger takes his love for both the franchise and the genre and channels them into something we've never really seen before," says Jake Kleinman. "Resident Evil is funny, scary, gross, and beautiful. Above all else, it captures the fight-or-flight experience of actually playing a Resident Evil game."

Gamespot (8/10): "By backing away from the stories and characters of the video games, Cregger dodges the giant bullet of 'that’s not my Leon Kennedy' and instead lets us finally experience Resident Evil ourselves, through our own eyes," says Eric Frederiksen.

(Image credit: Sony Pictures)IGN (8/10): "With a laser focus on putting its hero through the worst night of his life," Tom Jorgensen says, "Resident Evil is a simple and exciting survival horror story that benefits greatly from director Zach Cregger’s sensibilities."

Discussing Film (4/5): "Even though it’s an original story, Cregger’s take on Resident Evil sets a new high bar for video game movies by capturing the source material’s demented spirit while doing something clever and inventive with it.

Collider (8/10): "Clocking in at 90 minutes, Cregger's Resident Evil puts a lean, mean spin on an iconic horror franchise that's only poised to keep getting bigger, with a story that sits within the margins of the existing games while still giving fun, clever nods to its source material," says Carly Lane.

AV Club (B): "The 90-minute B-movie so deftly juggles gags and gross-outs that, when it’s finally boxed in by the larger demands of IP, it’s as tragic as watching a beloved character succumb to the dehumanizing effects of a virus."

(Image credit: Sony Pictures)Rolling Stone (Unscored): "Screw what hardcore fans say a movie adaptation should be," says Pie Conzaga. "Cregger’s take on RE is just as gross, funny, and scary as the games."

Variety (Unscored): "Is it a good movie?" asks Owen Gleiberman. "Let’s call it a sweetly executed piece of escapist trivia. It’s got a quirky relatability… for a Resident Evil movie."

The Hollywood Reporter (Unscored): "Cregger very much makes the film his own while displaying his obvious affinity for the source material," says Frank Scheck. "He’s crafted a propulsive, simultaneously terrifying and hilarious thrill ride that showcases both his cinematic chops and perverse sense of humor."

(Image credit: Sony Pictures)A few more quotes? Lisa Laman of Land of the Nerds says "Resident Evil is automatically up there with Exit 8 and Sonic the Hedgehog 3 as the best live-action video game movie ever made," Donald Clark of the Irish Times says "Cregger’s shameless romp, though smallish in scale, feels like the best Resident Evil film in the franchise’s long history," and Adam Olinger of Adam Does Movies (YouTube review) calls it "the best videogame movie of all time."

items.text:
It's been a good while since we last heard about Balatro's big 1.1 update—a year, almost to the day, since developer LocalThunk delayed it into 2026. There's still no sign of it, but the community did catch sight of LocalThunk yesterday when he popped into the Balatro Discord to let everyone know that everything is going fine.

"I'm happy the leaks are going over so well," LocalThunk wrote, referring to teases about the 1.1 update that he's been posting himself. For instance:

(Image credit: Localthunk (Discord))"I know you guys want to know as much as possible about 1.1 but I can't give away too much. I know it's taken a very long time and I've completely blown past the 2025 time frame but I promise I'm cooking in the way that is both best for me and ultimately for the game."

That tracks back to LocalThunk's 2025 message about the 1.1 delay, in which he said he became "well and truly burned out" after going too hard for too long on Balatro's development. After taking an extended break, he "very slowly" eased back into the work and was approaching more like a hobby developer, avoiding deadlines and not "trying to force things creatively." He also expressed regret for announcing the then-2025 release target for the 1.1 update, a point he reiterated in his new message.

"I understand how frustrating that must be and I wish I could go back in time and slap some sense into myself," LocalThunk continued. "At the time it was still go-go-go and I never even considered that I could allow myself to stop, then after mobile came out I was just so burnt out I couldn't touch the game for a bit. Luckily things have changed."

(Image credit: Localthunk (Discord))Consequently, LocalThunk said he'll continue to turn up in the Balatro Discord now and then to reassure people that the 1.1 update is still in development, and maybe post some more "leaks," but there won't be any commitment to a release target until it's ready to go. He also made clear that despite knowing people may be frustrated by the long wait, he's not going to speed things up: "I don't want this to be half baked and wreck Balatro, I love the game too and I want to play a fun game not a rushed botch job."

"I truly am having the best time making the game now. This past year of dev has been probably the most fulfilling work I've ever done, including pre launch times when it was a little hobby project," LocalThunk concluded. "I'm trying to keep offline as much as possible because that's a recipe that works well for me but I'll ease back in when 1.1 is ready to go."

People on the Balatro Discord, for the record, showed no sign of the frustration or impatience LocalThunk is concerned about: Most of the responses expressed happiness that he's doing well and encouraged him to take his time with it. One apparent newcomer to the Discord was particularly excited by the mere appearance of the dev:

(Image credit: Sighanora (Discord))For Balatro heads eager for information on what the update will contain, LocalThunk shared more than just the 'four Jokers' tidbit above. The major points are collected in this Reddit thread: A tier 2 voucher named Lunker, algorithmic changes for picking the next voucher, a blue stakes rework, and that sort of thing. What really leapt out to me, though, is that LocalThunk expects the 1.1 update to be the end of the road: After the 1.1 update comes, a 1.1.1 update will follow "for balance tweaks and changes after player feedback."

"That's likely it," he wrote. "Don't expect any more than that." He also confirmed that Balatro will not be getting a multiplayer mode.

It should go without saying at this point, but I'll say it anyway: The Balatro 1.1 update sounds like it will be big, but there's absolutely no indication as to when it will arrive.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?

items.text:
Mario Harik is the CEO of XPO, one of the largest logistics companies in the world.

For years, he was the protege of legendary entrepreneur Brad Jacobs (who built eight multibillion-dollar companies from scratch). Today, Mario leads 40,000 people with a management style shaped by what he learned. It’s a rare combination of smart capital allocation, discipline, deep listening, and a genuine belief in human potential.

Mario shares how he uses real-time data and second-order thinking to make better decisions faster, how he hires and develops A players (and the test that instantly tells you who isn’t one), how he runs meetings that pull the best thinking out of the most junior person in the room, what he learned working alongside one of the best entrepreneurs of our generation, and why ego, complacency, and small goals are quietly capping everything.

I hope you enjoy this conversation as much as I did.

Featured clips

Letting go of perfection and understanding how people operate

Learning from frontline employees and feedback loops

Analytical approach to risk and decision-making

Creating a high-performance environment through belief and feedback

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript

+ Check out the Granola notes.

Tiny Lessons

“If you set big goals, you achieve great things. If you set small goals, you achieve small things.”

“Ego is thinking you’re so good at something that you stop learning.”

“I worry if I’m in a team meeting and everybody’s aligned on a solution.”

In meetings, senior people speak last.

“A lot of leaders spend time on the output. You’ve got to spend time on the inputs.”

Tell people what to do but not how. When you tell them how, you set the ceiling at your best idea not theirs.

If somebody quits and your feeling is ‘whew, that’s good news’ — you should have gotten rid of them long ago.

“Most people think at the speed of speech. You can train your mind to go much faster.”

“When I give constructive feedback, I never make it subjective. I always ground it on data.”

“A lot of what people flag as potential issues ends up being why somebody fails at work.”

Yearly performance reviews are theater. “Performance reviews should be done on a daily and weekly basis.”

Don’t stop at the first answer. Double and triple-click.

The three variables that matter most when hiring: “Are they good at what they do? Are they serious about work? Are they kind?”

“It’s okay to have some friction.”

“Disagree all you want. Just focus on the problem, not the person.”

“Winning breeds winning.”

“Life is short. You’ve got to set big, big goals.”

“If you want to create alpha, don’t settle for a local maximum.”

“My hobbies are my work and my kids.”

“Every morning you have a choice: do the job the way you always do it, or learn new things.”

The only competition is yourself. “The bar isn’t beating the competition. The bar is: are we achieving the best we can achieve?”

“Work is part of life, the same way life is part of work.”

“When you show someone you believe in them, they have much higher odds of being great.”

“Every person in their own way is beautiful. Your job is to find how their mind works, not flatten it.”

“The biggest lever in business is who’s on the team and how they work with each other.”

items.text:
The anticuchos at Cholapink. | Cholapink

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).

September 11

A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.

An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.

An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died

Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.

Fall restaurant season is HERE

Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.

An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address

Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.

Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.

Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.

A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.

A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.

September 4

A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn

Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.

Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.

The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.

Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.

Two NYC restaurants take over Times Square Red Lobster

A restaurant group behind NYC restaurants, including American brasserie the Smith and pizzeria Parla, is taking over the recently shuttered Red Lobster in Times Square, as reported by the New York Post. The business plans to open a fifth location of the Smith and a pizza-slice spinoff of Parla at a two-floor address at 582 Seventh Avenue, between West 41st and 42nd streets, set to debut in 2028.

We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter (please sign up if you haven’t already!), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out August, July, and June’s).
September 11
A new Peruvian spot from a chef and a rapper

Peruvian chef Jaime Pesaque (of notable Lima restaurant Mayta) and Puerto Rican rapper Daddy Yankee (yes) are teaming up to open a new fast-casual Peruvian restaurant in New York City this fall. Cholapink is opening at 32 Spring Street, near Mott Street, in Nolita in October. The menu highlights grilled street food, also known as anticuchos, with ajis (marinades and sauces) like miso-glazed chicken thighs, pineapple gochujang pork belly, yuzu-amarillo fish, and spicy peanut mushrooms.
An NYC taco fave gets private equity funding

NYC’s favorite taqueria chain Los Tacos No. 1 is getting investment money from private equity firm TSG Consumer Partners, as reported by QSR. After the news was announced, people took to commenting on Los Tacos’ Instagram page, worrying about potential quality issues and increased prices (see: the discourse about Salt Hank’s acquisition by food hall behemoth Wonder). The team responded, assuring that they’re “definitely not messing with the tacos,” and that the reason they took the investment is so that they can “keep getting better at it” and expand. The restaurant recently partnered with Gap on an apparel collaboration.
An NYC artist and restaurant owner has died
Lucien Smith, the NYC artist who had revived iconic Chinatown restaurant Food, has died at the age of 37, as reported by Cultured. The restaurant had posted last week that it was temporarily closing.
Fall restaurant season is HERE
Bad news: Summer is unofficially over. Good news: it’s fall preview season! Part one of Eater NY’s most anticipated restaurant openings of the fall is on the website; part two is over on Substack.
An anticipated Hong Kong-style diner finds its address
Turns out chef Lucas Sin is indeed opening his dream cha chaan teng Lok Kee at M Star Cafe in Chinatown, where he’d been popping up this late summer.
Mrs. and Mr. Swift’s NYC night out

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce dined at Ambassadors Clubhouse on Saturday, September 6, per a rep for the fancy Indian restaurant in Nomad. They dined in one of the private dining rooms, enjoying drinks and food. I’d bet they ordered the tableside whiskey cocktail, the Patiala Peg.
Top Chef winner pops up with bodega preview

Chef Danny Garcia continues previewing his forthcoming Latin halal restaurant, Only Goods, with a pop-up bodega this weekend. It’s taking place at 307 Bedford Avenue, near South Second Street in Williamsburg on Saturday, September 12, from 1 to 5 p.m.
A kaiseki anniversary party

Tribeca kaiseki Muku is celebrating its first anniversary with a special tasting menu this fall, featuring dishes like a rare Japanese sweetfish and harako meshi, a dish of white rice, salmon, and roe. The $375 menu is available through Saturday, October 3.
A 10-year-restaurant collab celebration

To celebrate Fish Cheek’s 10th birthday, the restaurant is teaming up with other NYC restaurants and bars for special collaboration dishes. Starting on Saturday, September 12, find the choo chee michelada and zapp popcorn chicken at Lower East Side cocktail bar Double Chicken Please; the razor clams with nam jim seafood at American Asian Hudson Square restaurant Kiko; the clam pie at both the East Village and Bushwick locations of Ops Pizza; and sliced flaky Thai coconut cake at sibling gluten-free Nolita bakery Bub’s. And then, starting on Monday, September 14, there’s a special burger at Prospect Heights Jewish bistro Gertrude’s.
September 4
A Vietnamese American bakery returns to Brooklyn
Some good news: After baker Doris Hồ-Kane shuttered her Vietnamese American bakery in February, she’s working on bringing back Bạn Bè to its original Carroll Gardens neighborhood.
Hồ-Kane launched a Kickstarter campaign to help fund the opening. She’s aiming to open in November at 115 Columbia Street, at Kane Street, in the Columbia Street Waterfront District.

The resurrected space will have a takeout window and a first-time indoor dine-in space. On deck are pastries and sweets like the beautiful bright-green pandan honeycomb cake and new stuff like pandan lime madeleines and pandan chocolate tiramisu. For savory vegeterian items, look for banh mi, Vietnamese crepes, and summer rolls, along with coffee and tea drinks.
The McNally son ventures into the restaurant world

Keith McNally’s son, George, opens his Tribeca restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3, at 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable.
Buy stellar baked goods for a good cause

Expert baker Natasha Pickowicz is hosting a community bake sale this weekend to raise money for Queens nonprofit Make the Road New York. Our Little Bake Sale features chefs like Pickowicz herself, Zoë Kanan of Elbow Bread, Morgan Knight of Saint Street Cakes, Flynn McCarry of Cove, Ali Domrongchai, and many others. It’s free to attend; each pastry is worth one ticket, which is $10. The event, which is a partnership with indie food publication Cake Zine, takes place on Sunday, September 6, from 3 to 5 p.m. at Little Island, the park on Pier 55 along Hudson River Park at West 13th Street.
